podcast.body: Neil Young wrote "Ohio" in about an hour after David Crosby showed him a photo spread of the Kent State shootings in Life magazine. The song directly blamed Richard Nixon for the May 4, 1970 shooting of 12 unarmed students by the Ohio National Guard, a response to Nixon's April 30, 1970 announcement of a preemptive strike in Cambodia. David Crosby called it "the bravest thing he had seen in music," and the band (CSNY) assembled in Los Angeles to record it. "Ten soldiers and Nixon's coming were finally on our own this summer I hear the drummen for Dead in Ohio."

A protest song recorded with Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young, against the 1970 violence at Kent State. It barely qualifies as a diss record because Neil Young, as the songwriter, calls out President Richard Nixon by name. "Crosby Stills' Nash and Young's Ohio, a protest against the 1970 violence at Kent State barely qualifies as a disc record since songwriter Neil Young calls out President Richard Nixon by name."

podcast.body: Written in May 1970, this song was a direct response to the outrage felt after four protesting students were tragically killed by National Guard troops at Kent State University. The speed of its creation and release was remarkable, as it was on sale and on the radio within a month of the incident. Lyrics include: "Ten soldiers and Nixon coming, we're finally on our own. This summer I hear the drumming for dead in Ohio. Gotta get down to the rain." "Neil Young was so outraged that he wrote the song Ohio, and it was on sale and on the radio within a month."
